tasks.short: Design the routine or database, write the code, test it, review it, deploy it to the web GIS server, and document it.

steps.what: GIS technician designs the software routine or GIS database
GIS technician develops specialised software routines and internet-based GIS databases

loop.input: The technician's description of the change and the existing code.
loop.output: Draft code changes and unit tests.
loop.check: The tests must pass and the technician reviews every changed line and checks that it does what the design says, not only that tests pass, before it is kept.
loop.stop: Up to three attempts per change; then the technician writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Code templates cover only the boilerplate.

steps.what: GIS technician tests the routine by hand on test data
GIS technician reviews the final code before release
GIS technician merges the reviewed code, and the pipeline deploys it to the web GIS server: deployed by hand today
GIS technician documents the routine for users and colleagues
GIS technician checks the final documentation against the deployed routine: what it does, inputs, outputs and limits
GIS technician publishes the checked documentation for users and colleagues

tasks.design: A coding assistant drafts code changes and unit tests from the technician's description; tests must pass and the technician reviews every changed line. The tests run automatically in the build pipeline ({OTHER}) instead of testing by hand on each change. Once the technician has reviewed the final code, the technician merges it and the pipeline deploys it to the web GIS server. Documentation starts from the code comments and a page template; the technician writes it, checks it and publishes it. Designing the routine stays with the technician.
tasks.previous_blocker: Code, tests and deployments were all done by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Coding assistants draft code and tests; pipelines test and deploy.
tasks.still_hard: Drafted code can look right and still be wrong for spatial edge cases.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing a data model that will still work in five years.
tasks.altitude: The technician reviews drafted code instead of typing all of it.

evidence.claim: Field trials with 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm found 26% more completed tasks with an AI coding assistant.
In a randomised trial, 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools; the authors call it outdated.

assumptions: Boundary: from agreed requirements to the routine documented; gathering requirements is outside.
Input contract: repository and pipeline available; fallback is coding and deploying by hand.
The technician reviews every changed line.
s5 keeps 10 for merging and watching the deploy. s6 keeps 75: the page template and code comments give the structure, but the explanation for users is the technician's own writing.
research_questions: Does review time eat the time saved on drafting?

already_counted.description: GIS technician reviews drafted code changes.

incremental.description: GIS technician maintains the build pipeline.

approvals.approved_version: The code exactly as reviewed by the technician in s4, merged once and deployed by the pipeline to the web GIS server; any later change needs a new review.
The routine's documentation exactly as checked by the technician in s6b against the deployed routine, published once on its documentation page; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: complex spatial routines where drafts often fail, so s2 keeps 95, and many cases still need testing by hand, so s3 keeps 85 (10.5); high: simple database and web forms as designed (21.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Meet users to discuss their needs, show alternatives with example maps and apps, write the requirements, and explain the effort of each alternative.

steps.what: GIS technician assists users in formulating GIS requirements in meetings
GIS technician shows alternatives by searching for example maps and apps
GIS technician writes the requirements document
GIS technician explains the implications and effort of each alternative

tasks.design: A gallery of earlier maps, viewers and apps with short descriptions ({DOCS}) lets the technician show alternatives without searching old projects. A requirements template with fields for data, users, scale, update rate and output guides the write-up, and a standard effort table per product type gives the implications of each alternative. Meeting users stays with the technician.
tasks.previous_blocker: Examples were searched in old projects and requirements written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Shared galleries and templates are simple to keep in the team wiki.
tasks.still_hard: Users often do not know what they need until they see it.
tasks.human_edge: Turning a vague wish into a map that answers the real question.

evidence.claim: Galleries of earlier products and requirements templates can be kept in a team wiki.

assumptions: Boundary: from the user need to implications explained; building the product is outside.
Input contract: gallery and effort table kept by the GIS team; fallback is searching old projects.
Meetings do not get shorter. s3 keeps 80: the template gives fields for data, users, scale, update rate and output, but the technician still writes the requirements.
research_questions: Do requirements change less after work starts?

incremental.description: GIS technician adds finished products to the gallery.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: new kinds of products with no gallery examples or effort figures, so s2 and s4 keep 90 (8.0); high: variations on known products as designed (17.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Decide topics and level, write exercises and handouts, prepare sample datasets, make slides, and give the training or presentation.

steps.what: GIS technician decides training topics and level
GIS technician prepares training materials with exercises and screenshots

loop.input: The technician's outline and the steps recorded by a screen step recorder.
loop.output: Draft exercises with numbered steps and screenshots.
loop.check: The technician runs every exercise in the GIS software with the sample data and edits steps that do not work.
loop.stop: One draft per exercise; if rejected, the technician writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: The step recorder gives raw clicks, not explained exercises.

steps.what: GIS technician prepares sample datasets for the exercises
GIS technician makes presentation slides
GIS technician makes presentations to GIS users

tasks.design: A screen step recorder captures the technician's clicks with screenshots, and a bounded step turns them and the outline into draft exercises; the technician runs every exercise and edits it. Sample datasets and slides are kept in a shared training library ({DOCS}) and reused. Deciding topics and giving the training stay with the technician.
tasks.previous_blocker: Exercises and screenshots were made by hand for each course.
tasks.enabler_now: Step recorders capture screenshots; language models draft steps from them.
tasks.still_hard: Software updates change screens and break exercises.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing which user is lost and helping them back on track.
tasks.altitude: The technician tests exercises instead of writing them from scratch.

evidence.claim: TOPdesk drafts knowledge items for review.
Language models can draft exercise steps from recorded screenshots and an outline.

assumptions: Boundary: from the training request to training given; course evaluation is outside.
Input contract: training library kept by the GIS team; fallback is writing from scratch.
The technician runs every exercise before use.
s2 keeps 65: clicks and screenshots are captured by the step recorder, but the technician still writes the explanations and runs and edits every exercise.
research_questions: How much of each drafted exercise is kept?

already_counted.description: GIS technician runs and edits drafted exercises.

incremental.description: GIS technician updates exercises after software updates.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a new course on a new tool, so little can be reused from the library (s3 and s4 keep 90) and drafted exercises need much rework (s2 keeps 85) (8.5); high: an update of an existing course (27.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read release notes, test the new version with the organisation's data and tools, decide the recommendation, write it, and present it.

steps.what: GIS technician reads release notes of new GIS software and equipment
GIS technician tests the new version with the organisation's data and tools
GIS technician considers the implications and decides the upgrade recommendation
GIS technician writes the upgrade recommendation
GIS technician makes recommendations regarding upgrades to the IT manager

tasks.design: Release notes and compatibility lists of the GIS products in use arrive in one feed ({OTHER}), so the technician does not visit vendor sites. A set of test scripts for the organisation's key processing models and web maps runs on a test server with the new version and lists what breaks, instead of trying each workflow by hand. The recommendation uses a template. Deciding and presenting the recommendation stay with the technician.
tasks.previous_blocker: Release notes were searched on vendor sites and workflows tested by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Test scripts rerun key workflows on a new version.
tasks.still_hard: Plug-ins from small vendors break without notice.
tasks.human_edge: Judging whether an upgrade is worth the disruption now.

reach.learn: Whether risks are known in advance.

evidence.claim: Test scripts can rerun key GIS workflows on a new software version and report failures.
Organisations under the national cyber security law must keep systems secure, including timely updates.

assumptions: Boundary: from the new version to the upgrade recommended; carrying out the upgrade is outside.
Input contract: test server and scripts kept by the GIS team; fallback is manual testing.

The recommendation decision stays with the technician. s1 keeps 80: reading stays, visiting vendor sites drops. s4 keeps 80: the template gives the structure, but the reasoning is written by the technician.
The IT manager's time does not change.

incremental.description: GIS technician keeps test scripts current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: major upgrades with many changes the scripts do not cover, so s2 keeps 85 (12.2); high: routine minor updates as designed (17.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The GIS technician keeps designing routines, discussing needs, deciding training topics and upgrades; hand-typed code, manual tests, searched examples and hand-made exercises shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A technician with more time on design.

job.title: Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians
